title: The armies; the conch shells (1.1–1.19)
hook: a blind king asks what happened on the field, and a man with borrowed sight begins to tell him

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa: a practice small enough to survive a Tuesday. Your line was a practice that fits. Today, a new camp, and a book.

The Bhagavad Gita's first voice isn't Krishna's or Arjuna's. It's an old blind king, far from the battle, asking a question. In Edwin Arnold's translation from 1885: "Ranged thus for battle on the sacred plain— On Kurukshetra—say, Sanjaya! say What wrought my people, and the Pandavas?" Camp four is that book, the Song of the Lord, read in order over eleven weeks. Eighteen chapters; tradition counts seven hundred verses. You met its people in the stories: the Pandava brothers, their cousins the Kauravas, Krishna taking the reins of Arjuna's chariot on the eve of war. The Gita begins right there.
screen: `A BLIND KING ASKS.` → `WHAT WROUGHT MY PEOPLE?` → `CAMP FOUR: ONE BOOK, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: The king is Dhritarashtra, father of the Kauravas. He can't see, and he isn't on the field. The sage Vyasa has given his minister, Sanjaya, the sight to see the whole battle from the palace. So the entire Gita is a report, told to a blind father who already fears the answer. His first words: Dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah. On the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, gathered, eager to fight. Two names at once: a real place, Kurukshetra, north of Delhi, where pilgrims still go, and dharmakshetra, the field of dharma, of what's right. Sanjaya begins. Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, walks up to his old teacher Drona and lists warriors, ours and theirs, a little too fast, like someone nervous talking over the silence. Then old Bhishma, the great-uncle, roars like a lion to cheer him and blows his conch shell. The whole field answers: conches, drums, horns, all at once. On the other side, in a great chariot yoked to white horses, Krishna and Arjuna blow theirs. Krishna's is Panchajanya. Arjuna's, Devadatta. Bhima's, the giant one, Paundra. Every brother has his own. The sound, Sanjaya says, tears at the hearts of the Kauravas and echoes through earth and sky. Many readers, Gandhi among them, have heard the field as more than a place: a human life, where the right and the easy line up and face each other. Either way, the book starts where your hard days start. Everyone's in position. The noise is deafening. Nobody has moved yet.
screen: `A REPORT TO A BLIND FATHER.` · `THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` · `A LIST TOO FAST, THEN THE CONCHES.` · `THE FIELD IS A LIFE, TOO.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S IN POSITION.`

segments.voice: Picture a wide plain at dawn, lined up with the things you're facing right now: a decision, a person, a deadline, a fear. Let the noise come, the conches and drums and every voice in your head at once, and don't fight it; just hear it. Underneath, notice your breath, still going, steady, like Sanjaya quietly telling what he sees: nobody has to move yet.
The armies. Two sides of one family, lined up on Kurukshetra, the field of dharma, and a roar of conch shells before anyone moves.
Your line: the field. Day one hundred fifty-seven, and the book is open.

howItsDone: Many Hindus read or chant the Bhagavad Gita at home or in study groups, often a chapter at a time; the whole text is framed as Sanjaya's report to the blind king Dhritarashtra, and chapter one opens on the field of Kurukshetra.
